title: HE HEALED OTHERS… BUT GOD ALLOWED HIM TO DIE SICK. WHY?
paragraphs: HE HEALED OTHERS… BUT GOD ALLOWED HIM TO DIE SICK. WHY?

The heartbreaking final chapter of Elisha reveals a truth about suffering, unanswered prayers, and God's faithfulness that many Christians are afraid to confront. And if you have ever begged God to heal someone you love, only to watch them grow weaker, this story may change the way you understand faith forever.
There is a kind of pain that becomes almost impossible to explain.

It happens when you have prayed until your voice trembles. When you have fasted. When you have believed. When you have reminded God of His promises, held on to every Scripture about healing, and waited for the miracle you were certain would come.
But the hospital monitor keeps beeping.
The medical results keep getting worse.
The person you love keeps growing weaker.
And eventually, somewhere between another sleepless night and another unanswered prayer, a question escapes your lips.
"Lord… why?"
Not because you have stopped believing.
But because you still believe, and you cannot understand what God is doing.
You have heard testimonies of people being healed. You have watched others celebrate miraculous recoveries. You have read about the blind receiving sight, the lame walking, and the dead being raised.
Yet the person you are praying for is still suffering.
Perhaps that person is you.
And the hardest part is not always the illness itself.
Sometimes it is the silence surrounding it.
The silence of people who promised that your healing was coming.
The silence after someone confidently declared that your miracle was already done.
The silence when you wonder whether you did something wrong.
Whether you lacked faith.
Whether God is disappointed in you.
Whether the prayers that seemed powerful enough for everyone else somehow stopped working when they reached your hospital room.
Now imagine something extraordinary.
Imagine being one of the greatest miracle-working prophets in Israel's history.
Imagine seeing poisoned water made clean, a widow's desperate financial situation transformed, a dead child restored to life, and a man suffering from leprosy cleansed.
Imagine witnessing the power of God so unmistakably that kings, soldiers, widows, and ordinary families knew the Lord was working through you.
Then imagine lying on your own deathbed.
Sick.
Weak.
Dying.
And the God who performed so many miracles through your ministry does not deliver you from that final illness.
That was Elisha.
And what Scripture says about his death may confront some of the most dangerous assumptions Christians have made about healing.
Because there is something more disturbing than the fact that Elisha became sick.
It is the fact that the Bible makes absolutely no attempt to hide it.
"Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died." — 2 Kings 13:14, KJV
Read that again.
Elisha.
The prophet who had witnessed extraordinary miracles.
The man who carried on Elijah's prophetic ministry.
The servant of God through whom remarkable healings had occurred.
He became sick.
And he died from that sickness.
No dramatic explanation.
No accusation that he had secretly sinned.
No statement that his faith had weakened.
No suggestion that God had abandoned him.
Just a painfully honest sentence.
Elisha became ill, and that illness led to his death.
And perhaps the reason this verse unsettles us so deeply is that it exposes something we have quietly started to believe.
That if God truly loves us, He will always heal us.
That if our faith is strong enough, sickness cannot overcome us.
That if we serve Him faithfully, our bodies will somehow be exempt from the suffering experienced by everyone else.
But Elisha's death stands in Scripture like a witness against those assumptions.
Not against God's power.
Not against God's goodness.
But against the idea that every faithful servant of God is promised physical healing before death.
And to understand why this matters, we need to look more closely at the words Scripture actually uses.
In the Hebrew text of 2 Kings 13:14, we encounter this expression:
וֶאֱלִישָׁע חָלָה אֶת־חָלְיוֹ אֲשֶׁר יָמוּת בּוֹ
Ve’Elisha chalah et-cholyo asher yamut bo.
A close translation is:
"Now Elisha had become sick with the illness from which he would die."
The Hebrew verb חָלָה (chalah) means to be sick, become weak, or suffer illness, depending on its context.
The related noun חֳלִי (choli) refers to sickness or disease.
The phrase אֲשֶׁר יָמוּת בּוֹ (asher yamut bo) identifies the illness as the one from which he would die.
The language is remarkably direct.
The inspired narrator does not present Elisha's sickness as an illusion. It was not merely a symbolic spiritual battle. It was a real physical illness with a fatal outcome.
And there is another detail we must not overlook.
The Bible never tells us what specific disease Elisha had.
It does not tell us how long he suffered.
It does not record the prayers he may have prayed for his own recovery.
It does not explain why God did not heal him.
And it certainly does not authorize us to invent a secret sin, a spiritual failure, or some hidden curse to explain his death.
Sometimes faithfulness to Scripture requires the humility to stop where Scripture stops.
But there is more to this account.
Because while Elisha was dying, something extraordinary happened.
King Jehoash of Israel came down to see him.
And when the king looked at the dying prophet, he wept.
"My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof." — 2 Kings 13:14, KJV
These words echo what Elisha himself had cried when Elijah was taken from him in 2 Kings 2:12.
The king recognized that Israel was losing someone whose prophetic ministry had been profoundly important to the nation.
But here is the detail that should make every reader stop.
Elisha was physically dying, yet God was still speaking through him.
The illness had weakened his body.
It had not invalidated his prophetic calling.
The king came to a dying man, and through that dying man, God delivered a message concerning Israel's conflict with Syria.
Elisha instructed the king to take a bow and arrows.
Then the prophet placed his hands upon the king's hands.
He told him to open the eastward window and shoot.
And when the arrow flew, Elisha declared:
"The arrow of the LORD's deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria." — 2 Kings 13:17, KJV
Think about that.
The prophet could not escape his own approaching death, but he could still announce God's promised deliverance for his people.
His failing body did not mean God had finished using him.
His illness did not mean his ministry had been meaningless.
His approaching death did not erase the truth he had proclaimed.
And there is a deeply personal message here for anyone who has begun to believe that being sick makes them spiritually useless.
You may no longer have the strength you once had.
You may need help getting out of bed.
You may no longer be able to serve in church the way you used to.
You may feel embarrassed that others now have to care for you.
But please hear this.
Your physical weakness does not make your life worthless in the kingdom of God.
Your dependence on others is not evidence that you have become a burden to Christ.
You are not less loved because you need medication.
You are not less faithful because you need treatment.
And you are not spiritually defeated simply because your body is struggling.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony in a room comes from the person who can barely stand but still whispers, "Jesus, I trust You."
Not because suffering is automatically holy.
Not because pain should be romanticized.
But because genuine faith can remain alive even when physical strength is disappearing.
And this is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
After Elisha died, he was buried.
Then, according to 2 Kings 13:20–21, something happened that sounds almost impossible.
While some men were burying another man, they saw a band of Moabite raiders approaching.
In their urgency, they placed the dead man's body into Elisha's tomb.
And when that body touched Elisha's bones, the man revived and stood upon his feet.
Yes.
The prophet who had died from an illness became associated with one final extraordinary miracle after his death.
But we must be careful with what this passage actually teaches.
It does not say that Elisha possessed independent supernatural power in his bones.
It does not instruct believers to seek healing through human remains.
It does not promise that every burial place of a faithful servant will become a place of miracles.
The account describes an extraordinary event recorded by Scripture, demonstrating that death had not rendered God's power ineffective.
The miracle belongs to God.
And there is a striking contrast that the biblical narrative invites us to consider.
Elisha died.
Another man was raised.
The prophet's own death was not reversed in that moment.
Yet God's power to give life was displayed.
The Lord was never dependent upon Elisha's continued physical existence to accomplish His purposes.
And perhaps this is one of the most uncomfortable truths we need to recover.
God's power is not measured by whether He performs the particular miracle we desperately want.
That sentence may hurt.
Especially if you are reading this beside someone who is dying.
Especially if you have already buried someone you begged God to save.
Especially if you have heard well-meaning Christians say that every unanswered healing prayer must reveal a lack of faith.
But Scripture will not allow us to make that accusation so easily.
Consider the apostle Paul.
He pleaded with the Lord three times concerning what he called a thorn in his flesh.
We are not told exactly what that thorn was, so we should not confidently identify it as a particular disease.
But we are told that Paul wanted it removed.
And the Lord answered:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not tell Paul that every difficulty would immediately disappear.
He did not promise that weakness would never touch him again.
Instead, Christ revealed the sufficiency of His grace in the very place where Paul felt inadequate.
That does not mean God never heals.
He does.
The Scriptures testify to His power to heal, and Christians are instructed to pray for the sick.
James 5:14–16 calls believers to prayer and care within the community of faith.
But prayer is not a mechanism by which human beings force God to perform a predetermined outcome.
Faith is not a currency we accumulate until heaven owes us a miracle.
And healing is not a prize awarded only to Christians who have achieved some superior spiritual status.
If that were true, what would we say about Timothy?
Paul advised him:
"Use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." — 1 Timothy 5:23, KJV
Timothy had recurring health problems.
Yet Paul did not simply accuse him of unbelief.
What would we say about Trophimus?
"Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick." — 2 Timothy 4:20, KJV
Paul, through whose ministry God had performed extraordinary miracles, acknowledged leaving a fellow worker sick.
What would we say about Epaphroditus?
Philippians 2:27 tells us he had been sick and near death, but God had mercy on him.
Here, Scripture explicitly celebrates recovery.
These passages belong together.
One servant becomes sick and dies.
Another struggles with recurring ailments.
Another is left sick.
Another becomes gravely ill and recovers.
The biblical record does not force every faithful believer's physical condition into one predictable formula.
And that matters.
Because somewhere tonight, a mother is blaming herself for her child's illness.
A husband is wondering whether his wife's condition would improve if he prayed more intensely.
A young Christian is afraid to tell anyone about a diagnosis because someone might accuse them of harboring unbelief.
An elderly believer is quietly asking whether decades of serving Jesus were somehow insufficient.
And someone who has lost a loved one is carrying not only grief but also guilt.
They are wondering whether their prayers failed.
If that is you, please listen carefully.
The death of someone you love is not, by itself, proof that you failed them spiritually.
You can pray sincerely and still grieve.
You can believe in God's healing power and still seek medical treatment.
You can trust Christ deeply and still weep at a graveside.
And you can love God with your whole heart while admitting that you do not understand why a particular healing never came.
Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
John 11:35 gives us two of the shortest and most emotionally revealing words in Scripture:
"Jesus wept."
He knew what He was about to do.
He knew Lazarus would rise.
And still, He wept.
The Son of God did not treat human grief as an embarrassment.
He entered it.
He stood among mourners.
He saw their sorrow.
And He wept.
So why do we sometimes make grieving Christians feel ashamed for crying?
Why do we tell the suffering to stop asking questions when Scripture contains lament after lament from people who loved God?
Why do we sometimes speak as though tears are evidence of weak faith?
Jesus never needed to apologize for His tears.
And neither should you.
But there is an even deeper question beneath Elisha's illness.
If God had the power to heal him, why did God allow him to die?
The answer requires both courage and humility.
Scripture does not reveal God's specific reason for allowing Elisha's final illness to end in death.
We should not pretend otherwise.
But Scripture does reveal a larger truth about the human condition.
Hebrews 9:27 reminds us that human beings are appointed to die once and afterward face judgment.
Romans 5:12 explains that sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin.
Death is part of the fallen human condition.
It is an enemy, not a friend to be celebrated.
First Corinthians 15:26 explicitly calls death "the last enemy."
Even those who experience miraculous healing remain mortal unless the Lord returns first.
A healed body is still a body awaiting final redemption.
Lazarus was raised from the dead, but the Bible does not teach that he became permanently immune to mortality.
Every healing in this present age, however wonderful, is temporary in comparison with the resurrection life Christ promises His people.
And here we come to the heart of the Gospel.
Because Elisha's story ultimately points us beyond Elisha.
Beyond prophetic miracles.
Beyond the question of why one faithful man died sick.
It directs our attention toward the only Savior who has decisively conquered death.
Jesus Christ.
The One who healed the sick.
Opened blind eyes.
Cleansed lepers.
Restored the broken.
Called Lazarus out of the tomb.
And then willingly walked toward His own death.
Think about the scandal of the cross.
The One who gave life to others submitted Himself to death.
The One who had the authority to command the winds and waves allowed Himself to be arrested.
The One who healed wounded bodies permitted His own body to be pierced.
The One who could call upon heavenly help chose obedience to the Father's saving purpose.
People mocked Him.
They challenged Him to save Himself.
Matthew 27:42 records their cruel accusation:
"He saved others; himself he cannot save."
They thought His refusal to come down from the cross proved His weakness.
But the cross was not the failure of His mission.
It was central to the mission He came to accomplish.
He was not dying because He had lost control.
He was giving Himself for sinners.
And unlike Elisha, Jesus was not merely a servant through whom God performed miracles.
He is the incarnate Son of God, the promised Messiah, the Savior who bore our sins and rose victorious from the grave.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"With his stripes we are healed."
The Hebrew expression is:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
Uvachavurato nirpa lanu.
A close translation is:
"And by His wound, healing has come to us."
The context of Isaiah 53 concerns the suffering Servant bearing the sins and iniquities of others.
First Peter 2:24 applies this passage to Christ, explaining that He bore our sins in His body on the tree so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.
That is crucial.
The healing accomplished through Christ's suffering must never be reduced to a guarantee that every Christian will immediately recover from every physical disease.
His saving work addresses the deepest devastation caused by sin and secures the ultimate redemption of His people.
And yes, that redemption includes the body.
Romans 8:23 speaks of believers awaiting the redemption of their bodies.
First Corinthians 15 proclaims the resurrection of the dead.
Revelation 21:4 promises a future in which God will wipe away every tear and death will be no more.
The Gospel does not promise that every believer will escape sickness today. It promises that everyone who belongs to Christ will share in His final victory over death.
That is not a smaller hope.
It is an infinitely greater one.
Because what good would it be to survive one illness if death still held eternal dominion over us?
What good would it be to gain a few more years if sin still separated us from God?
Jesus came to accomplish something greater than temporarily extending our earthly lives.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
To forgive the guilty.
To redeem the lost.
To bring the spiritually dead to life.
To open the way to eternal fellowship with the Father.
And through His resurrection, He established the certainty of the future resurrection of those who belong to Him.
That is why Christian hope can survive even at a graveside.
Not because the grave is harmless.
Not because separation does not hurt.
Not because believers are required to smile through devastating loss.
But because the empty tomb of Jesus declares that death will not have the final word.
And perhaps now we can understand something about Elisha that we could not understand at the beginning.
His illness did not cancel God's faithfulness.
His death did not invalidate his ministry.
His grave did not place God's power beyond reach.
And his story was never meant to teach us that faithful people are exempt from mortality.
It teaches us that even the greatest servants of God remain dependent upon the God they serve.
Elisha was never the source of the miracles.
God was.
Elisha was never the Savior.
Jesus is.
And this distinction changes everything.
Because if your faith is ultimately anchored in a miracle, what happens when the miracle does not come?
If your confidence in God depends entirely on receiving the outcome you want, what happens when the diagnosis changes?
If you believe God's love can only be measured by the absence of suffering, how will you understand the cross?
The cross reveals a love that entered suffering to redeem sinners.
And the resurrection reveals a power that suffering and death could not defeat.
That is where our confidence belongs.
Not in our ability to explain every tragedy.
Not in our ability to predict every healing.
Not in the intensity of our emotions.
But in the crucified and risen Christ.
Maybe you are reading this while fighting an illness that has exhausted you.
Keep praying.
Ask others to pray with you.
Seek appropriate medical care.
Receive help without shame.
Rest when you need rest.
And do not allow anyone to convince you that taking medicine is a betrayal of faith.
Maybe you are caring for someone whose condition keeps worsening.
Love them.
Sit beside them.
Hold their hand.
Pray with them if they welcome it.
Tell them what they mean to you.
Do not spend every precious moment trying to manufacture the perfect declaration that will guarantee recovery.
Sometimes the ministry God places before us is simply to remain present in love.
And maybe you have already experienced the loss you begged God to prevent.
You prayed.
You believed.
You waited.
And the funeral still happened.
You have replayed the final days in your mind more times than you can count.
What if you had prayed differently?
What if you had fasted longer?
What if you had recognized the symptoms sooner?
What if you had found another doctor?
Some of those questions may deserve thoughtful attention, especially where practical decisions were involved.
But do not turn every unanswered question into an accusation against your own faith.
God has not given us permission to judge the spiritual worth of a person by the manner of their death.
Elisha's final illness should make us much more careful about the words we speak over suffering people.
And much more compassionate toward those whose prayers seem unanswered.
There is something profoundly Christlike about refusing to add shame to another person's pain.
There is also something deeply courageous about admitting:
"I still believe God can heal. But I do not know what He will do in this situation."
That is not unbelief.
That is faith refusing to pretend it knows what God has not revealed.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop hiding behind the words, "I'm fine."
You are not fine.
You are exhausted.
You are afraid.
You are grieving.
You have been trying to appear spiritually strong while quietly falling apart.
You keep encouraging everyone else, but when the room becomes silent, your own heart begins to ache.
If that describes you, there is room for your honesty before God.
The Psalms are filled with cries of anguish, confusion, longing, and desperate dependence.
God's Word does not require you to pretend that suffering feels pleasant.
You can tell Him the truth.
You can say, "Lord, I am afraid."
You can say, "I don't understand."
You can say, "Please heal me."
You can say, "Help me trust You."
And when your strength is nearly gone, you can pray the words of the father who cried out to Jesus in Mark 9:24:
"Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
That is a prayer worth remembering.
Because sometimes faith does not sound like a triumphant declaration.
Sometimes it sounds like a trembling confession from someone who desperately wants to believe.
And Christ is not confused by the difference.
There is another kind of sickness, however, that we must not ignore.
The sickness of a heart separated from God by sin.
You may be physically healthy and spiritually far from Christ.
You may have years ahead of you and still be living without repentance.
You may know every Christian song, recognize every famous Bible verse, and appear respectable before people while quietly resisting the Lord who calls you to surrender.
And perhaps that is why this story matters so urgently.
Elisha's death reminds us that earthly life is not permanent.
Not even for the faithful.
Not even for the powerful.
Not even for those who have witnessed extraordinary miracles.
The question is not merely whether you will experience healing in this life.
The deeper question is whether you have been reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Have you repented of your sins?
Have you placed your trust in the crucified and risen Savior?
Are you relying on His grace, or are you still trying to establish your own righteousness?
The Gospel does not say that good people earn eternal life by being religious enough.
It announces that sinners can be forgiven through Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our works.
Romans 10:9 speaks of confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead.
And 1 John 1:9 assures us of God's faithfulness and righteousness in forgiving those who confess their sins.
This is not an invitation to perform spirituality for an audience.
It is an invitation to come honestly before God.
To stop hiding.
To turn from sin.
To trust Christ.
To receive the mercy you could never purchase.
If your heart is stirring right now, you can pray:

"Lord Jesus, I have spent so much of my life wanting Your blessings while struggling to surrender to Your will. Forgive my sins. Forgive my pride. Forgive the ways I have misunderstood Your goodness. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You when I understand and when I do not. Heal what You will in my life, strengthen me through what I must endure, and keep my heart anchored in You. I surrender myself to Your grace. In Jesus' name, amen."
And if you prayed that sincerely, do not stop at an emotional moment.
Open the Scriptures.
Learn the Gospel.
Join a faithful local church.
Seek mature Christian fellowship.
Grow in prayer.
Let the truth of Christ shape how you live, love, suffer, forgive, and serve.
Because discipleship is not merely about feeling inspired for a few minutes.
It is about following Jesus through the ordinary and extraordinary moments of life.
Through celebration and disappointment.
Through strength and weakness.
Through answered prayers and difficult waiting.
Through seasons of abundance and seasons when all you have left is the promise that Christ will never forsake His people.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish emotional stories.
Not to turn Scripture into entertainment.
Not to promise a life without suffering.
But to keep pointing wounded, searching, struggling, and growing souls back to Jesus Christ.
To proclaim biblical truth in a world filled with confusion.
To encourage repentance without withholding grace.
To remind the weary that the Gospel is not exhausted by their failures.
To help believers become more deeply rooted in the Word of God.
And to keep announcing the message that stands at the center of everything we do:
That message is not a promise that every earthly circumstance will turn out the way we imagined.

It is the announcement that through Jesus Christ, guilt can meet forgiveness, rebellion can meet mercy, sinners can become children of God, and even death itself will ultimately give way to resurrection.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture more clearly, strengthened you through suffering, or encouraged you to return to Christ, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
But because Gospel-centered ministry requires people who are willing to help sustain and expand the work.

Some believers may prayerfully consider such support part of their broader Christian giving, alongside their responsibilities to their local church and those in need. But it should never be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe or presented as a replacement for faithful local-church stewardship.
It is the opportunity to help make more biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to others.
These resources are part of our desire to help people do more than simply read a powerful article and move on.
We want them to know Christ.
To understand Scripture.
To grow in discernment.
To become more prayerful, more humble, more compassionate, and more faithful in everyday life.
And please remember something important.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Think about the person who has just received a frightening diagnosis.
The family grieving a death they cannot understand.
The believer who has been told their illness proves they lack faith.
The Christian who feels spiritually abandoned because healing has not come.
Someone may need to hear that suffering does not automatically mean divine rejection.
Someone may need to rediscover that the hope of Christianity rests not in escaping every earthly hardship but in belonging to the Savior who conquered death.
But before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not a question designed to make you look spiritual.
A question that deserves an honest answer.
Have you ever prayed desperately for someone to be healed, only to face an outcome you could not understand?
You do not have to share details that are too painful or private.
If you have a testimony of God's comfort, healing, or sustaining grace, consider sharing it. Your experience may encourage someone else, even though no two journeys unfold in exactly the same way.
And if you are still wrestling with difficult questions, you are welcome to say that too.
This should be a place where people can speak truthfully about suffering without being shamed for their tears.
Because somewhere in these comments, a stranger may discover that they are not the only one who has cried through a prayer.
And perhaps that simple discovery will encourage them to seek Christ rather than turn away from Him.
Now return with me, one last time, to Elisha's deathbed.
The room is quiet.
The prophet is weak.
His earthly journey is nearing its end.
The king is weeping.
There is no recorded promise that the illness will disappear.
No statement that Elisha's faith has failed.
No explanation of every mystery.
But God has not ceased to be God.
The Lord's promises to His people have not been erased.
And the death of His servant cannot prevent Him from accomplishing His purposes.
Elisha's body will be buried.
Years of prophetic ministry will come to an end.
Yet the story of God's power will continue.
And centuries later, another tomb will enter the story of redemption.
A tomb outside Jerusalem.
A tomb where the body of Jesus Christ is laid after His crucifixion.
A tomb that will not hold Him.
On the third day, the crucified Savior rises.
Not merely restored to a few more years of mortal life.
But raised in victory, never to die again.
And in His resurrection, the ultimate answer to death begins to shine with unmistakable clarity.
Elisha could not prevent his own death.
Jesus conquered death.
Elisha was a faithful servant.
Jesus is the risen Lord.
Elisha's story reminds us that even God's servants are mortal.
Jesus' resurrection assures those who belong to Him that mortality will not have the final victory.
And that is why we can pray for healing without pretending that we control the outcome.
Why we can mourn without surrendering all hope.
Why we can stand beside a hospital bed and still believe that Christ is worthy of our trust.
Why we can acknowledge the terrible reality of death while holding firmly to the promise of resurrection.
The final Christian hope is not that our bodies will never become weak.
It is that the risen Jesus Christ will one day raise His people into life beyond the reach of sickness, sin, and death.
So if you are still waiting for healing, may you receive grace for today.
If you are caring for someone who is suffering, may Christ strengthen you in love.
If you are grieving, may the God of all comfort meet you in your sorrow.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, may you hear His call to repentance and faith while there is still time.
Because the greatest miracle you need is not merely the extension of your earthly life.
It is reconciliation with the living God through Jesus Christ.
Elisha's final illness leaves us with a mystery Scripture does not fully explain.
But the empty tomb of Jesus gives us a promise Scripture boldly proclaims.
Death is real.
Suffering is real.
Grief is real.
And Christ is risen.

The illness may have taken Elisha's final breath, but it could never take away the God who held his life—and the risen Christ is the reason death will never have the final word over those who belong to Him.
